title: Delhi RERA: How Homebuyers File Complaints, and the Unsettled Fight Over DDA Projects
subtitle: Delhi runs the same central RERA Act as every other state through its own 2016 Rules and its own Authority, and a long-running argument over whether the Delhi Development Authority counts as a promoter at all shows how unsettled parts of that regime still are.
meta_description: A working guide to the Delhi RERA complaint and appeal process, and where the fight over the Delhi Development Authority's registration currently stands.
author: Bhaskar Subramanian, Adv. Rahul Jangra
author_role: Partner, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors; Associate, S&S Co. Advocates & Solicitors
standfirst: Delhi buyers complaining about a delayed flat or a defaulting promoter follow the same central statute that applies everywhere in India, filled in locally by Delhi's own 2016 Rules and its own Authority. What does not follow a settled pattern is a four-year argument over whether the Delhi Development Authority, the single largest seller of housing and institutional plots in the capital, is even a promoter within the meaning of that statute, an argument that has produced registrations, penalties and a pending High Court petition without yet producing a final answer.
key_points: Delhi's complaint and appeal process runs on the central Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016, supplemented by the National Capital Territory of Delhi Real Estate (Regulation and Development) (General) Rules, 2016, notified on 24 November 2016.

Delhi did not get a full-time regulator until a notification dated 14 November 2018 named retired IAS officer Vijay S. Madan as the first Chairperson, and the Authority and its Tribunal now also serve Chandigarh.

The Delhi Development Authority spent years arguing it was not a 'promoter' under the Act, then registered 18 ongoing projects between 2022 and after an Authority order to cure deficiencies, while separately challenging the registration requirement itself before the Delhi High Court.

A complaint for refund, possession or interest goes to the Authority on Form M, while a claim for compensation under Sections 12, 14, 18 and 19 goes to the Adjudicating Officer on Form N, and reported fee figures for each differ across guides.
Whether a RERA complaint is subject to any limitation period at all is unsettled; a Chhattisgarh High Court ruling in 2026 held that it is not, but no Delhi ruling on the point was found.

An appeal to the Real Estate Appellate Tribunal requires the promoter to pre-deposit the amount the order requires it to pay, a condition the Supreme Court upheld as constitutional in Newtech Promoters and Developers Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P.
Both the Delhi Authority's chairmanship and Tribunal posts have run vacant for stretches, prompting the Delhi High Court in September 2026 to direct the Delhi government to speed up appointments.

sections.heading: A capital that runs its own version of a national law
paragraphs: Every state and Union Territory in India administers the Real Estate (Regulation and Development) Act, 2016 through its own regulatory authority, its own appellate tribunal and its own set of rules made under Section 84 of the central Act. Delhi is no exception to that structure, and most of what governs a complaint filed here, the forms, the two-track split between refund claims and compensation claims, the right of appeal, traces back to the same central statute that a buyer in Pune or Lucknow would rely on.

Two things make Delhi worth a guide of its own. The first is a set of local Rules and administrative choices, the date the Authority actually started functioning, the fact that it now also serves Chandigarh, that change some of the practical mechanics without changing the underlying law. The second, and the more consequential one, is a years-long dispute over whether the Delhi Development Authority, which has sold more housing stock in the capital than almost any private developer, is a promoter under the Act at all. That dispute runs through much of what follows, because it shapes how registration, penalty and appeal actually play out for a government seller rather than a private builder.

sections.heading: The framework: a central Act, a local set of Rules, and a late start
paragraphs: The National Capital Territory of Delhi Real Estate (Regulation and Development) (General) Rules, 2016 were notified by the Ministry of Urban Development as G.S.R. 1085(E) on 24 November 2016, under the rule-making power in Section 84 of the central Act. These Rules supply the Delhi-specific detail that the Act leaves to each government to fill in: the forms a complainant uses, the service conditions of the Tribunal's Chairperson and Members, and the fee schedule for an application. A later notification, G.S.R. 553(E) dated 1 July 2026, amended a table in Rule 32(1) to reflect the Jan Vishwas (Amendment of Provisions) Act, 2026, which decriminalised a category of minor compliance lapses under several central statutes, a reminder that the Rules are still being updated rather than frozen in their 2016 form.

Having Rules on paper and having a functioning regulator are different things, and Delhi took almost two years to close that gap. The permanent Authority was constituted by a notification issued under Section 20 of the Act and dated 14 November 2018, which named retired IAS officer Vijay S. Madan as Chairperson, with Gyan Prakash Srivastava and Ramesh Chandra as the other members. Contemporaneous press coverage described this as Delhi finally getting a full-time real estate regulator, implying that whatever arrangement existed before that date was, at best, provisional. The Authority's jurisdiction was subsequently extended to the Union Territory of Chandigarh as well, so a single Chairperson and a single Appellate Tribunal now serve both territories, a fact worth knowing before assuming every order or vacancy notice relating to Delhi RERA concerns Delhi alone.

That late start matters for how this Authority has behaved since. A regulator that spent its first two years simply getting staffed has had less time than some of its counterparts to build up a settled body of practice on harder questions, limitation being one of them, and that gap shows up later in this piece.

sections.heading: Who must register, and the argument that DDA should not have to
paragraphs: Section 3 of the Act requires a promoter to register a real estate project with the Authority before advertising, marketing, booking, selling or offering it for sale, subject to the size threshold set out in the provision, broadly a plot area above 500 square metres or more than eight apartments across all phases. Delhi RERA's own leadership has stated publicly that no category of promoter is exempt from this requirement, naming the Delhi Development Authority and the Delhi State Industrial and Infrastructure Development Corporation specifically as entities expected to register like any other seller.

DDA resisted that position for years. Its argument was not a technical quibble about paperwork; it went to the root question of whether a statutory development authority, selling flats and plots under its own allotment scheme and policed by its own internal quality mechanisms, is a 'promoter' within the meaning the Act gives that term at all. In December 2021 the Authority issued an order directing DDA to cure deficiencies in registration applications it had by then filed, an order that itself implies DDA had already begun applying, under protest, rather than refusing outright. Between August and September 2022, reports place DDA's registration of 18 of its ongoing housing projects with Delhi RERA.

Registering did not end the dispute, and it came with a cost. A contemporaneous trade report said Delhi RERA imposed a penalty of roughly Rs 1 lakh per project on DDA for delay in filing the registration applications, and separately fined 12 of the 18 projects Rs 25 lakh each over delay in submitting supporting documents. That report's precise publication date could not be confirmed in this research, and no second independent source was found repeating the exact figures, so they are given here as reported rather than as verified fact, and any party relying on the amounts should check Delhi RERA's own orders directly.

The deeper legal question outlived the registrations. DDA moved the Delhi High Court challenging the registration requirement itself, and in 2025 Justice Sachin Datta issued notice to Delhi RERA and the Union of India on that petition. Nothing in the available reporting suggests the petition has since been decided. The practical result is an odd straddle: DDA has, for now, gone on registering and operating under the regime it is simultaneously asking the High Court to say does not bind it, and anyone dealing with a DDA project today is dealing with an authority whose registration status is settled in practice but not in law.

DDA's underlying objection has a certain logic to it, even if it has not carried the day. A statutory authority built for slum clearance, land development and planned public housing sits a long way from the commercial builders Parliament most obviously had in mind when it drafted a definition of 'promoter' around construction for sale and allotment against consideration. DDA's own submissions have leaned on its internal quality control processes, flat inspection regimes and grievance mechanisms as a substitute for RERA oversight, essentially an argument that it already regulates itself adequately. Delhi RERA's answer has been institutional rather than doctrinal: it has simply treated DDA as covered, demanded registration, and left the constitutional and statutory arguments to be tested wherever DDA chooses to raise them, which turned out to be the Delhi High Court rather than the Tribunal.

sections.heading: Two forums inside one Authority
paragraphs: A Delhi complainant's first choice is not between RERA and some other body, but between two tracks within RERA itself, and picking the wrong one wastes a hearing date rather than a limitation period. A claim for possession, for a refund of the amount paid with interest, or for a direction that the promoter comply with the agreement, ordinarily under Section 18, goes to the Authority itself on Form M.

A claim for compensation, as opposed to refund or interest, is adjudicated separately. Sections 71 and 72 give that jurisdiction to an Adjudicating Officer appointed under the Act, and the complaint there is filed on Form N, covering compensation claims that can arise under Sections 12, 14, 18 and 19 of the Act depending on the facts, structural defects, misrepresentation in advertising, or a promoter's other defaults. Published guides disagree on the exact fee for each form, some giving a Form M fee range of roughly Rs 1,000 to Rs 5,000 and a Form N fee that one source puts at a flat Rs 5,000 and another puts at Rs 500 to Rs 2,000 depending on claim value. Given that disagreement, the only safe course is to confirm the current fee on Delhi RERA's own portal before filing rather than rely on any third-party guide, including this one.

The practical difference between the two tracks shows up most clearly in a straightforward delay case. A buyer who simply wants the flat handed over, or the money back with interest for the period of delay, is better served filing on Form M before the Authority, since that is the forum Section 18 itself contemplates for refund and interest. A buyer who also wants damages for a specific, quantifiable loss caused by the promoter's conduct, lost rent on an existing home during the delay, for instance, or the cost of repairing a structural defect under Section 14, needs the Adjudicating Officer's compensation jurisdiction on Form N for that separate head of claim, and the two can be pursued together where the facts support both.

sections.heading: Filing a complaint: the mechanics
paragraphs: Complaints are filed online through the Authority's portal, and the sequence that follows is broadly the same whether the complaint goes to the Authority or to the Adjudicating Officer: the respondent promoter is served with notice, the promoter files a written response, the matter is listed for one or more hearings, and a reasoned order follows. Documents that matter most at this stage are the allotment letter or builder-buyer agreement, every payment receipt, and the written correspondence in which the promoter acknowledged delay or made representations about possession, since orders under Section 18 turn heavily on dates fixed in the agreement against dates actually achieved.

A complainant does not need an advocate to be heard. Section 56 of the Act allows a person to appear before the Authority, the Adjudicating Officer or the Appellate Tribunal in person or through an authorised representative, a provision carried over from the Act's general design to keep the forum accessible without mandatory representation. That said, nothing in the provision stops a complainant from engaging counsel, and the practical value of doing so tends to rise sharply once a matter moves past a straightforward delay claim into anything involving disputed facts, set-off claims by the promoter, or an appeal.

Expect the promoter's response, too, to raise its own set of defences before the merits are even reached: force majeure clauses tied to events such as the pandemic years, delay attributed to the authority that cleared the project rather than to the promoter, or an argument that the complainant is itself in default on payment instalments. None of these defences are automatically fatal to a complaint, but a buyer who has kept a clean record of timely payments and written reminders about possession is in a far stronger position to meet them than one relying on memory and a single allotment letter.

sections.heading: How long you have to file: a question without a Delhi answer
paragraphs: Buyers often assume a three-year limitation period applies to a RERA complaint, borrowing the general residuary period under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963. Whether that assumption is correct is now genuinely contested. In April 2026, the Chhattisgarh High Court, in Nidhi Sao v. Greenearth Infraventures, held that Section 31 of the Act prescribes no period of limitation for a complaint filed before the Authority or the Adjudicating Officer, and that Article 137 accordingly does not apply to such complaints; the court set aside a lower order that had treated a complaint filed roughly three years and four months after the cause of action as time-barred. The Haryana Real Estate Regulatory Authority has reached a broadly similar conclusion on at least one occasion, holding that the three-year period applicable to a specific-performance suit under the Limitation Act does not carry over to a RERA complaint.

That position is not uniform even within the state that produced the leading ruling. A separate Chhattisgarh RERA order is reported to have applied a three-year limit to a claim for recovery of maintenance charges, suggesting the 'no limitation' principle may be confined to the kind of possession and refund claims Section 31 was built around, rather than extending to every category of dispute a party might bring before the Authority. Nothing in the material reviewed for this piece addresses the question specifically for Delhi, whether from Delhi RERA itself or from the Delhi High Court, so a Delhi complainant cannot safely assume the Chhattisgarh reasoning will be followed here. The only sound practical advice is to treat the Chhattisgarh ruling as a useful argument of last resort for an old claim, not as licence to delay a fresh one.

A related but distinct point concerns delay in filing an appeal rather than the original complaint. Section 44 itself allows the Appellate Tribunal to condone a delay beyond sixty days where the appellant shows sufficient cause, so a missed appeal deadline is not automatically fatal the way a missed civil suit deadline often is, though a party should never treat that discretion as a safety net and should calendar the sixty-day period from the date of the order, not from the date the order is actually received or read.

sections.heading: Appeal to the Real Estate Appellate Tribunal
paragraphs: A party aggrieved by an order of the Authority or the Adjudicating Officer may appeal to the Real Estate Appellate Tribunal within sixty days under Section 44, with the Tribunal empowered to admit a late appeal on sufficient cause being shown. Where the appellant is the promoter, the proviso to Section 43(5) requires it to deposit, at a minimum, thirty per cent of the amount determined by the order under appeal, or the entire amount payable to a specific allottee, whichever is less, before the appeal is entertained. The Supreme Court upheld that pre-deposit requirement against a constitutional challenge in Newtech Promoters and Developers Pvt. Ltd. v. State of U.P. (neutral citation 2021 INSC 716, decided on 11 November 2021 by a bench of U.U. Lalit, Ajay Rastogi and Aniruddha Bose JJ.), reasoning that a promoter holding a buyer's money is in a different position from an ordinary appellant and that the condition is not so onerous as to violate Articles 14 or 19(1)(g) of the Constitution.

In Delhi's case, this Tribunal does double duty, since it serves Chandigarh as well as the National Capital Territory, and it has not always been fully staffed. Advertisements inviting applications for a vacant Member post went out in both 2024 and 2025, and the regulator side of the house has had its own staffing gap: in 2026, after the Delhi government rejected a proposal on 11 August to extend the outgoing Chairperson's tenure, the post of Chairperson stood vacant alongside a Judicial Member post, leaving the Authority to function with only a technical member for a period. Two advocates approached the Delhi High Court over this, and in September 2026 the Court directed the Delhi government to expedite the process of filling the vacancies so the Authority and Tribunal could function as intended. Whether those appointments have since been made was not confirmed in the material available for this piece, and a complainant or appellant should check the current composition of both bodies before assuming either is fully constituted.

sections.heading: A further appeal to the High Court: less settled than most guides suggest
paragraphs: Section 58 of the Act provides for a further appeal to the High Court, and a great many secondary guides describe it simply as a second appeal from an order of the Appellate Tribunal, available within sixty days on a question of law. The caselaw is less tidy than that description suggests. At least one Bombay High Court ruling has read Section 58 narrowly, holding that it permits an appeal to the High Court only against an order of the Adjudicating Officer passed under Section 30, not against an order of the Appellate Tribunal passed under Section 43(5), and a Rajasthan High Court order has separately observed that Section 58 does not itself specify whether the appeal it creates operates as a second appeal in the ordinary procedural sense.

The practical consequence is that a party unhappy with a Tribunal order in Delhi cannot assume a straightforward statutory route to the High Court exists for every kind of order, and should take advice on whether the specific order falls within whatever reading of Section 58 a Delhi court would adopt, a question this research did not find settled one way or the other for Delhi specifically. Separately, and on firmer ground, an order of the Authority exercising its administrative or regulatory functions, as opposed to its adjudicatory ones, remains open to challenge by writ petition under Article 226, which is the very route DDA itself used to contest the registration requirement. The two routes, statutory appeal and writ, are not interchangeable, and choosing between them depends on the character of the order being challenged rather than on which route feels more familiar.

sections.heading: RERA, the consumer forum and the civil court
paragraphs: Section 79 of the Act bars a civil court from entertaining a suit or proceeding over a matter the Authority, the Adjudicating Officer or the Appellate Tribunal is empowered to decide, but the Supreme Court has confirmed in other proceedings, reported on this firm's own site under the heading of the Kabra Associates ruling, that this bar does not extend to a consumer commission, so a homebuyer in Delhi genuinely has a choice between RERA and the consumer forum for many delay and defect claims.

That choice, once made and argued on the merits, tends to stick. Courts have generally held a complainant to the forum they elected once they have gone past the preliminary stage and argued the substance of the claim there, rather than allowing a second attempt in the other forum over the identical grievance. A Delhi buyer weighing RERA against the Delhi State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission should treat that election as close to final in practice, whatever the formal position on concurrent jurisdiction, and choose the forum best suited to the relief actually wanted before filing rather than after an adverse order.

sections.heading: Execution: an order is not the end of the matter
paragraphs: Winning before the Authority, the Adjudicating Officer or the Tribunal does not by itself put money in a complainant's account. Section 40 of the Act allows an unpaid amount due under an order to be recovered as an arrear of land revenue, through a recovery certificate issued to the District Magistrate or Collector having jurisdiction over the promoter's assets, a mechanism this firm has covered separately and in more detail, and which Delhi complainants should expect to use in any case where the promoter does not pay voluntarily once an order becomes final.

sections.heading: What this means in practice
paragraphs: For a buyer or allottee with an existing grievance against DDA, the practical position today is that DDA has registered the bulk of its ongoing housing schemes and is, for most purposes, operating inside the RERA regime it is simultaneously contesting before the Delhi High Court. Nothing in that pending petition suspends DDA's existing registrations or stops anyone filing a fresh complaint, so there is no reason to wait for the writ petition to be decided before pursuing a delay, refund or compensation claim through the ordinary Form M or Form N process.

A private promoter in Delhi should take a different lesson from this episode, one that sits less in DDA's specific legal argument than in how Delhi RERA has conducted itself while that argument was pending: naming non-compliant promoters publicly, setting firm deadlines for registration, and imposing penalties for delay rather than waiting out a parallel legal challenge. A promoter weighing whether a project genuinely falls outside the registration threshold, or whether some other basis for exemption might apply, should assume Delhi RERA will test that position actively rather than accept it on the papers, and should be prepared to defend it with the same rigour DDA itself has had to bring to the Delhi High Court.

sections.heading: Delhi against the rest of the National Capital Region
paragraphs: A buyer who has looked at projects on both sides of the Delhi border will notice the regulatory map changes the moment the project crosses into Noida, Greater Noida or Ghaziabad. There, Uttar Pradesh RERA and the industrial development authorities created under state legislation sit alongside each other in a leasehold structure this firm has covered separately, and a buyer's underlying title often runs through an authority allotment rather than a simple sale deed, a structural feature Delhi largely does not share outside DDA's own schemes. Gurugram and Faridabad fall under Haryana RERA, a third regulator again, with its own case law on questions such as limitation that this piece has already drawn on for comparison.

The practical upshot for anyone transacting across the region is that the forum, the fee form and even a question as basic as whether a limitation period applies can change depending on which side of a municipal boundary the project happens to sit, even though the underlying Act is identical everywhere. This research did not find a reported standoff of the same scale and duration between a UP or Haryana development authority and its own state RERA, which is one reason DDA's four-year dispute with Delhi RERA stands out as unusual rather than as a pattern repeated across the region.

conclusion: Delhi's RERA machinery runs on the same central statute every other state uses, and most of the procedural questions a buyer or promoter faces here, which form to file, where compensation claims go, how an appeal works, have answers that would look familiar anywhere in the country. What sets Delhi apart at the moment is not a difference in the law but a difference in who is being asked to answer to it. A statutory development authority spent years resisting the label of promoter, lost that argument in practice if not yet in a reported judgment, and continues to litigate the underlying question in the Delhi High Court even while operating, project by project, inside the regime it disputes.

That unresolved overlay sits on top of an Authority and Tribunal that have themselves struggled with basic continuity, a late start in 2018, recurring vacancies through 2024, 2025 and into 2026, and on top of genuinely unsettled questions, limitation chief among them, that no Delhi ruling has yet answered. A complainant or a developer navigating this system in the capital does well to treat each of those three layers, the ordinary procedure, the DDA question, and the Authority's own staffing, as separate issues that happen to intersect in any given case, rather than assuming settled practice where none yet exists.

For anyone buying or litigating across the wider National Capital Region rather than inside Delhi alone, the deeper point is that this entire discussion resets at every state border. The same complaint that follows Form M and Form N before Delhi RERA follows a different authority, a different fee structure and, on at least the limitation question, potentially a different outcome once the project sits in Noida, Greater Noida, Ghaziabad or Gurugram, and treating the National Capital Region as one regulatory zone rather than four separate ones is the single most common mistake this firm sees in matters that cross those lines.

faqs.q: Is the Delhi Development Authority required to register its housing projects with Delhi RERA?
faqs.a: In practice, yes for now. DDA registered 18 of its ongoing housing projects with Delhi RERA between 2022 and the following year after the Authority directed it to cure deficiencies in its applications, but DDA has separately challenged the registration requirement itself before the Delhi High Court, and that petition had not been decided when this piece was prepared. The legal question remains open even though the practical position, for the time being, is that DDA's major ongoing projects are registered.

faqs.q: Should I file my complaint against a Delhi builder on Form M or Form N?
faqs.a: Form M goes to the Authority for possession, refund with interest, or a compliance direction, typically under Section 18. Form N goes to the Adjudicating Officer for a compensation claim under Sections 12, 14, 18 or 19. If you only want your money back with interest, Form M is usually the right route; if you are claiming compensation for a specific loss, such as a structural defect or a misrepresentation, Form N is the correct forum.

faqs.q: How much time do I have to file a RERA complaint in Delhi?
faqs.a: No Delhi ruling settling this was found. A Chhattisgarh High Court decision in 2026 held that no limitation period applies to a complaint under Section 31, and a Haryana RERA order has taken a similar view, but at least one Chhattisgarh RERA order applied a three-year limit to a different kind of claim, so the position is not uniform even in the state that produced the leading ruling. File as soon as the cause of action arises rather than relying on an argument that no deadline applies.

faqs.q: Do I need a lawyer to appear before Delhi RERA?
faqs.a: No. Section 56 of the Act allows a complainant or respondent to appear in person or through an authorised representative before the Authority, the Adjudicating Officer and the Appellate Tribunal. Representation becomes more valuable once the matter involves disputed facts, a promoter's set-off claims, or an appeal, but it is never mandatory.

faqs.q: What happens if the promoter does not pay after I win my complaint?
faqs.a: An unpaid amount under a final order can be recovered as an arrear of land revenue under Section 40 of the Act, through a recovery certificate issued to the District Magistrate or Collector with jurisdiction over the promoter's assets. This is a separate enforcement step that follows a favourable order; it is not automatic and generally needs to be applied for.

faqs.q: Can I go to the consumer forum instead of Delhi RERA?
faqs.a: Generally, yes, for many delay and defect claims, since the bar in Section 79 of the Act on civil courts has been held not to extend to consumer commissions. Once you argue your case on the merits in one forum, however, courts tend to hold you to that choice and will not entertain a parallel claim over the same grievance in the other, so decide which forum suits the relief you actually want before filing.

faqs.q: Is Delhi RERA fully staffed right now?
faqs.a: Not consistently. Both the Authority's Chairperson post and a Judicial Member post at the Appellate Tribunal have run vacant for stretches, most recently prompting the Delhi High Court in September 2026 to direct the Delhi government to speed up the appointment process. Check the current composition of the Authority and Tribunal before assuming either body is fully staffed when your matter is heard.

faqs.q: Does the Delhi Real Estate Appellate Tribunal also hear appeals from Chandigarh?
faqs.a: Yes. Delhi RERA's jurisdiction and its Appellate Tribunal were extended to cover the Union Territory of Chandigarh as well as the National Capital Territory of Delhi, so vacancy notices, appointments and some orders relating to this Tribunal concern both territories rather than Delhi alone.

verification_notes: The 24 November 2016 date and G.S.R. 1085(E) number for the Delhi Rules were confirmed from two independent sources, Taxheal's contemporaneous report and the text of the later 2026 amendment notification (G.S.R. 553(E)), which itself recites the original 2016 notification number and date.

The 14 November 2018 appointment of Vijay S. Madan as Delhi RERA's first Chairperson was confirmed from multiple independent contemporaneous sources (Business Standard/PTI, Square Yards, and Tribune India), which also agree on the other two members named at the time.

The penalty figures reported against DDA (roughly Rs 1 lakh per project and Rs 25 lakh each for 12 of 18 projects) came from a single contemporaneous trade report whose exact publication date could not be fixed and which could not be corroborated by a second independent source; they are presented in the text as reported rather than as independently verified, with an explicit caveat to that effect.

DDA's 2025 Delhi High Court petition and Justice Sachin Datta's notice were confirmed from a wire report (The Week/PTI) dated 10 June 2025; no later report confirming the outcome of that petition was found, and the article states plainly that the petition's result is unconfirmed as of the date of writing.

The Newtech Promoters citation (2021 INSC 716, decided 11 November 2021, bench of Lalit, Rastogi and Bose JJ.) and its holding on Section 43(5) were confirmed from two independent sources (K&K's case note and LawSathi's judgment page), both describing the same bench, date and outcome.

The Chhattisgarh High Court's Nidhi Sao ruling on limitation was confirmed from LiveLawBiz's report; a second, independent confirmation of the exact case number and date was not found in this research pass, so the holding is attributed to the reported source rather than to an independently opened judgment, and the article flags the limitation position as unsettled rather than stating it as settled law.

The September 2026 Delhi High Court direction on filling RERA vacancies was confirmed from two independent sources (Bar and Bench and SupremeToday.ai), corroborated by the Delhi High Court's own public notice dated 29 September 2026 inviting applications for the Chairperson post.

The reading of Section 58 as limited to Adjudicating Officer orders (rather than Tribunal orders) rests on one reported Bombay High Court ruling found through secondary sources; a second independent source was not located confirming the precise holding, so the article presents this as a documented point of uncertainty rather than as settled law, consistent with the conflicting commentary found on this question generally.

The reference to the Supreme Court's ruling on RERA's relationship with consumer forum jurisdiction (described in the text as the Kabra Associates ruling) relies on this firm's own previously published and verified coverage of that decision rather than fresh independent verification in this research pass.

Reported fee ranges for Form M and Form N complaints conflict across secondary sources and could not be confirmed against Delhi RERA's current fee schedule in this research pass; the article states the conflict explicitly and advises confirming current fees with the Authority directly rather than asserting a specific figure.
